concept.centerRule: A Scene belongs when a source materially distinguishes clean and unclean, commands or narrates washing or purification, declares a person or object clean, restores access, or interprets earlier cleansing language. Shared vocabulary never erases object, agent, status, moral claim, sequence, or outcome.

characterAnchors.label: Noah
characterAnchors.note: Receives clean and unclean animals and later offers from the clean animals.

characterAnchors.label: Moses
characterAnchors.note: Receives distinctions and procedures governing bodies, food, priests, sanctuary, camp, and restored access.

characterAnchors.label: Aaron and the priests
characterAnchors.note: Are washed for service and must inspect, distinguish, declare, teach, and administer restoration.

characterAnchors.label: Naaman
characterAnchors.note: Resists a simple washing command before returning from the Jordan cleansed.

characterAnchors.label: David
characterAnchors.note: Uses washing, hyssop, clean-heart, Spirit, presence, teaching, and sacrifice language in confession.

characterAnchors.label: Isaiah
characterAnchors.note: Names unclean lips and receives altar contact, removed guilt, forgiveness, and commission.

characterAnchors.label: Ezekiel
characterAnchors.note: Preserves cleansing promises involving water, heart, Spirit, people, altar, covenant, and sanctuary.

characterAnchors.label: Jesus Christ
characterAnchors.note: Touches and cleanses, sends people to priests, challenges handwashing traditions, and calls disciples clean.

characterAnchors.label: Peter
characterAnchors.note: Learns not to call people unclean and later speaks of hearts cleansed by faith and baptism’s evidence boundary.

characterAnchors.label: Paul
characterAnchors.note: Receives a baptismal washing command and teaches assemblies about food, conscience, identity, holiness, word, and Spirit.

concept.throughline: The trail moves from distinctions before Sinai through priestly and communal procedures, prayer and prophecy, Jesus’ cleansing acts and disputes, baptism and community boundaries, word, blood, Spirit, conscience, enduring life, and final access.

edges.basis: Genesis already distinguishes clean and unclean animals; Leviticus supplies detailed food and contact classifications. The earlier narrative assumes knowledge that it does not explain; the law later defines boundaries for Israel without narrating their origin.
edges.label: A distinction before and within Israel’s law

edges.basis: Both sources join selected animals to approach after a crisis of judgment. Noah’s offering follows the flood; Leviticus coordinates sacrifice, blood, confession, removal, and sanctuary cleansing.
edges.label: Clean animals offered and a sanctuary cleansed

edges.basis: Jacob’s household and James’s audience are summoned to abandon divided loyalties before approach. Genesis narrates gods removed and clothes changed; James addresses hands, hearts, grief, and humility.
edges.label: Purification before drawing near

edges.basis: Both passages connect washing language to drawing near while retaining boundaries and communal responsibility. Exodus imposes distance and timed preparation; Hebrews speaks of confidence, conscience, hope, and gathering.
edges.label: Washed bodies at two approaches

edges.basis: Priests and Levites undergo washing or purification before service. Aaron’s sons are washed, clothed, and anointed; the Levites receive cleansing water, shaving, washing, offerings, and presentation.
edges.label: Ministers prepared for service

edges.basis: Priests wash before sanctuary service, while Jesus washes disciples’ feet before commanding mutual service. The basin protects priestly approach; John distinguishes bathing, footwashing, participation, and Judas’s exception.
edges.label: Feet washed at the boundary of service

edges.basis: Leviticus defines a priestly responsibility that Ezekiel later says priests have violated. The charge is instructional in Leviticus and accusatory within a collapsed social order in Ezekiel.
edges.label: Priests charged to teach—and charged with hiding—the distinction

edges.basis: Both laws require washing while status continues until evening. Leviticus 11 treats carcass contact across food and vessels; Numbers 19 develops corpse contact, sprinkling, ashes, and exclusion.
edges.label: Washing that does not end uncleanness immediately

edges.basis: Luke locates Jesus’ presentation within the purification time and offering prescribed by the law. Leviticus defines the procedure; Luke compresses purification, presentation, firstborn language, and offering around Jesus.
edges.label: Childbirth purification commanded and narrated

edges.basis: The law gives priests the work of inspection and declaration; the Gospel narrates immediate cleansing followed by priestly testimony. The priest observes and declares status; Jesus touches and cleanses before sending the man to the priest.
edges.label: Priestly inspection and Jesus’ cleansing touch

edges.basis: Leviticus provides the staged restoration invoked by Jesus’ command to show the priest. The law spreads restoration across days and rites; Mark foregrounds immediate cleansing and disruptive publicity.
edges.label: Restoration procedure and a cleansed man’s public report

edges.basis: Both sources inspect built space and remove affected material rather than treating the structure as a person. A private house may be scraped or destroyed; the Temple is restored through ministerial consecration and removal.
edges.label: Uncleanness removed from house and Temple

edges.basis: Leviticus regulates bodily conditions and contact; Jesus argues that harmful actions from the heart defile a person. The passages address different objects and causes, so shared defilement language cannot make bodily status moral guilt.
edges.label: Bodily uncleanness and moral defilement

edges.basis: Both sources draw a boundary around divine dwelling. Numbers names temporary conditions and camp exclusion; Revelation presents the final city and a boundary tied to falsehood and the Lamb’s book.
edges.label: Uncleanness outside camp and outside city

edges.basis: People emerge from violent settings with cleansing of bodies, objects, or robes. Numbers prescribes water, fire, and time after war; Revelation gives a paradoxical image of robes whitened in the Lamb’s blood.
edges.label: Cleansing after conflict and through tribulation

edges.basis: Both passages tie what enters communal space to God’s presence there. Deuteronomy regulates camp life during war; Revelation imagines permanent light, open gates, and final exclusion.

edges.basis: Naaman and ten men receive cleansing while acting on a prophet’s or Jesus’ instruction. Naaman resists before washing seven times; the ten go toward priests, while one alone returns in thanks.

edges.basis: Both sources face people whose access is challenged by expected purification boundaries. Hezekiah prays for participants who lacked prescribed purification; Acts argues that God cleansed Gentile hearts by faith.

edges.basis: Both passages narrate purification linked to shared worship and communal perception. Ezra emphasizes ministers prepared for Passover; Acts presents Paul’s action amid contested reports that remain unsettled.

edges.basis: Nehemiah and Revelation place cleansing boundaries around a restored city. Nehemiah narrates dedication of people and structures; Revelation describes entry, glory, light, and exclusion.

edges.basis: Jeremiah commands Jerusalem to wash its heart; Peter says God cleansed Gentile hearts by faith. One is an urgent prophetic imperative before judgment; the other is testimony about divine action in a community dispute.

edges.basis: Jeremiah and Revelation connect cleansing language to restored public dwelling and witness among nations. Jeremiah promises cleansing and pardon for a ruined city; Revelation describes the final city’s entry boundary.

edges.basis: Ezekiel and Titus join washing or water language to the Spirit and transformed life. Ezekiel orders promised actions toward Israel and land; Titus gives a compressed argument about saving mercy, washing, and renewing.

edges.basis: Ezekiel and Titus describe God forming a people through cleansing or purification. Ezekiel emphasizes gathering, king, covenant, and sanctuary; Titus emphasizes redemption, identity, and good works.

edges.basis: Zechariah and 1 John place cleansing from sin beside ongoing communal conditions. Zechariah announces an opened fountain amid contested prophecy; 1 John relates light, fellowship, blood, confession, and truthfulness.

edges.basis: Malachi and Titus connect purification to the changed work of a people. Malachi focuses on Levites, offerings, and judgment; Titus speaks of a people zealous for good works.
edges.label: A purified people whose work becomes acceptable

edges.basis: Matthew and Mark preserve the same core encounter while selecting distinct aftermath details. Matthew foregrounds Moses’ offering as testimony; Mark foregrounds the man’s publicity and Jesus remaining outside.

edges.basis: Matthew and Mark preserve the movement from tradition and food to the heart and defiling acts. Mark includes a food-related aside; Matthew frames the disciples’ concern and explanation differently.

edges.basis: Matthew and Luke use vessel and interior imagery against visible religious performance. Matthew addresses scribes and Pharisees through woes; Luke begins from surprise during a meal and develops a distinct accusation sequence.

edges.basis: Adjacent Johannine scenes place purification objects or disputes near revelation about Jesus. Cana uses jars without explaining a complete symbolism; John’s disciples name a dispute that opens into bridegroom testimony.

edges.basis: John twice calls disciples clean while preserving different contexts and exceptions. Footwashing distinguishes bathing, participation, and Judas; vine teaching names Jesus’ word, pruning, abiding, and fruit.

edges.basis: Acts and Romans revisit clean/unclean language after the Gospel crosses communal boundaries. Peter’s vision develops toward people; Romans makes a claim about things while limiting action through conscience and love.
edges.label: Food language, people, and conscience

edges.basis: Acts and 1 Peter use washing or cleansing boundaries in baptismal speech. Acts gives a compact command to Paul; 1 Peter explicitly denies bodily dirt removal and names a good-conscience appeal.

edges.basis: Hebrews first compresses purification and enthronement, then develops blood, conscience, covenant, and offering. The opening does not explain the mechanism; chapter 9 builds an extended contrast between sanctuary service and Christ’s offering.

edges.basis: Peter and John connect cleansing language to ongoing communal life rather than a private status alone. Peter moves from obedience and purification to love and new birth; John holds fellowship, confession, blood, and truthfulness together.

edges.basis: 2 Peter looks backward to cleansing from former sins; Revelation looks toward washed robes and entry. One warns against blindness and forgetfulness in present growth; the other pronounces a final blessing with an outside boundary.
edges.label: Remembered cleansing and final access

edges.basis: Revelation twice relates washed robes to access in its final visions. Chapter 7 places the multitude before the throne after tribulation; chapter 22 ties washing to the tree and gates while others remain outside.
